_README: Real data, drawn from the extension manifests, READMEs and popup source on 28-29 Aug 2026. NOTE ON STATS: Facebook 243/394/77 (sponsored, follow, join) and Cookies 357/45/228 are REAL, read from chrome.storage in the author's own profile on 29 Aug 2026. The YouTube figures are ILLUSTRATIVE, chosen by the author rather than measured — the real profile held only a day's use, and 0.31.0 resets the first counter anyway. They are at least self-consistent under the fixed semantics: more videos protected than ads that got through, which the old code could not have produced because it incremented both counters on the same line. Do not describe them as measured anywhere. NOTE ON LABELS: the first YouTube stat is 'Videos protected', not 'Ads stopped'. From 0.31.0 it counts videos whose ad schedule was stopped before the player saw it, credited once per video. NOTE ON VERSIONS: `version` is the version the Chrome Web Store actually serves, checked on the public listing rather than taken from the local manifest, because the repos run ahead of the store. A releaseUrl is only kept where a GitHub tag matches that exact version, since the install button names the version it links to; YouTube and Facebook have no matching tag and so carry no releaseUrl, and their install button falls through to 'Get it on GitHub' naming nothing. Cookies points at v0.22.6. NOTE ON REPO NAMES: the repos are quite-for-youtube, quite-for-facebook and quite-for-cookies. Older yt-ad-cleaner / fb-feed-cleaner URLs only redirect. NOTE ON QUITE FOR INSTAGRAM: it is published on the Chrome Web Store but its source is not on GitHub, so it is deliberately absent from this file and has no page on the site. The privacy page names it through site.json's privacyExtra, and the 'you can check all of this' line lists only the extensions that have a githubUrl, so nothing claims a repo that does not exist. Add it here, with a githubUrl, if the source is ever published; the privacy sentence picks it up on its own and the privacyExtra entry then comes out.

_versionNotes.checked: GitHub API, 27 Aug 2026. Never use raw.githubusercontent.com — it serves a stale CDN cache.
_versionNotes.releases: Both repos are tagged (v0.20.8 / v2.5.4) and releaseUrl points at those tag pages, which carry GitHub's auto-generated source zip. Those zips are ~300 KB because they include test/ and repo metadata. package.sh builds a lean ~40 KB zip instead — attach it via 'Create release from tag' on GitHub and the download gets 7x smaller. Then releaseUrl can become /releases/latest.
_versionNotes.size: Reflects the GitHub source zip a visitor actually downloads, not the packaged extension.
_versionNotes.cookies: Store ships 0.22.0 and GitHub is tagged v0.22.0, so both routes now offer the same build. They were briefly out of step: the only tag was v0.20.0 while the manifest had moved to 0.22.0, which put an older build behind a button labelled 'latest release', directly under an Add to Chrome installing the newer one.
_versionNotes.facebook: Live on the store at 2.6.3 from 30 Aug 2026, and tagged v2.6.3 on GitHub, so both routes offer the same build. The earlier note about a two-extension cap is obsolete: a second publisher account is what unblocked the submission.
_versionNotes.youtube: Site names 0.31.8, which is what the GitHub release gives. The store is still serving 0.30.0 while 0.31.8 is in review, and the page notice says so. Before 29 Aug the page named 0.20.8, a version neither route delivered. Drop the notice once the store catches up.

extensions.name: Quite for YouTube
extensions.summary: Skips video ads and hides the ad panels in your feed, sidebar, search results and Shorts, without tripping YouTube's anti-adblock check.
extensions.metaDescription: Free, open-source Chrome extension that skips YouTube video ads and hides feed, sidebar, search and Shorts ad panels. One permission, no tracking.
description: Quite for YouTube deals with advertising in two places at once. Video ads are got past: Skip is clicked the moment it appears, and unskippable ads are fast-forwarded. The ad panels scattered through the homepage, sidebar, search results and masthead never paint at all, because they are hidden before the page renders.

There is a second setting, Strip ad schedule, which removes the ad list from the video's data before the player reads it. It works by declaring the player's request as an ad unit rather than a watch page, so nothing in YouTube's answer is edited after the fact. We spent a day trying to measure how many adverts that actually prevents and could not show a clear effect, so we no longer claim one. It is on by default and it does no harm; we would rather describe it than sell it.
extensions.requires: Chrome, Edge, Brave, Arc, Opera or another Chromium browser.

permissions.name: storage
permissions.why: To remember your checkbox settings, and a running count of what it has hidden or skipped. Settings use Chrome's own extension-settings sync, so with Chrome sync on they travel with your Chrome profile.

hostPermissions.name: *://*.youtube.com/*
hostPermissions.why: The extension runs on YouTube and nowhere else. It has no permission to read, or even see, any other site you visit.

features.title: Video ads, got past
features.body: Skip is clicked as soon as it appears and unskippable ads are fast-forwarded. Seeking is a last resort that never touches anything longer than three minutes, because that is not an ad.

features.title: Feed ads never paint
features.body: Homepage, sidebar, search results and the masthead banner are hidden before the page renders, so there is no flicker of an ad you then watch disappear.

features.title: Player overlays gone
features.body: The banners drawn on top of the video while you are watching it are removed along with everything else.

features.title: Merch shelves, if you want
features.body: Product shelves under videos can go too. Off by default, because some people actually use them.

features.title: Nothing is faked
features.body: The ad schedule is never edited after the fact, which is what keeps the session out of YouTube's anti-adblock net. Whether it also prevents adverts is something we tried to measure and could not demonstrate, so the listing no longer says it does.

features.title: Diagnostics built in
features.body: The popup shows the version actually running in the page and reports what it has done this session, with a Copy report button for when something needs looking at.

options.name: Protection
options.what: Master switch.

options.name: Strip ad schedule
options.what: Removes the ad list from the video's data before the player reads it.

options.name: Skip video ads
options.what: Clicks Skip, fast-forwards unskippable ones.

options.name: Hide feed & search ads
options.what: Homepage, sidebar, search, Shorts, masthead.

options.name: Hide player overlays
options.what: Banners on top of the video.

options.name: Hide merch shelves
options.what: Product shelves under videos.

options.name: Status badge
options.what: Troubleshooting overlay on the page.

faq.q: Why not just use a normal ad blocker?
faq.a: Network-level blockers trigger YouTube's anti-adblock wall. This works differently. It stops the ad schedule being issued rather than blocking the request afterwards. Running both at once is worse than running either, because you cannot tell which caused what.

faq.q: Will I still see an ad start?
faq.a: Briefly, sometimes. The default is to let the ad begin and then get past it. On one verified session of 37 live ads: 35 skipped, 2 fast-forwarded, 2 seeked, and no false seeks.

faq.q: It stopped working after a YouTube update.
faq.a: YouTube changes its player regularly, and skipping can break until the extension catches up. Expected rather than a regression. Click the icon to check the version actually running in the page, and reload the extension if it does not match what you installed.

faq.q: Does it work on Edge or Brave?
faq.a: Yes. It runs in Chrome, Edge, Brave, Arc, Opera and other Chromium browsers.

extensions.privacy: Quite for YouTube runs only on youtube.com and has no permission to access any other site. No server, no analytics, no account, no tracking, and nothing is sent to us. It stores the checkboxes you have ticked and a running count of what it has skipped or hidden. Settings use Chrome's own extension-settings sync, so with Chrome sync switched on they travel with your Chrome profile, the same as any extension's settings. There is also a diagnostic log that records which videos you hopped between, which is off unless you switch it on with ?ytachistory=1, and which Chrome clears when you quit.
extensions.metaTitle: Remove YouTube Ads: Quite for YouTube, Chrome extension
extensions.pitch: Skip is clicked the moment it appears and unskippable ads are fast-forwarded. The ad panels in your feed, sidebar, search results and Shorts never paint at all.

extensions.name: Quite for Facebook
extensions.tagline: A feed of the people you actually know.
extensions.summary: Takes ads, suggested posts, suggested groups and the Sponsored column out of your feed, and leaves your friends' posts exactly where they were.
extensions.metaDescription: Free, open-source Chrome extension that hides ads, suggested posts, suggested groups and the Sponsored column from your Facebook feed. No tracking.
description: Quite for Facebook strips out the things you never asked to see: posts marked Sponsored or Ad, pages you do not follow pushed into your feed, groups you are not a member of, and the ad panel sitting above your contacts on the right.

What it leaves alone matters just as much. Your own posts, your friends' posts, groups you are in and pages you already follow are never touched. Nothing is blocked, unfollowed or reported on your behalf. Posts are hidden from view, and everything comes straight back the moment you switch it off.

features.body: Anything marked Sponsored or Ad is hidden as the page builds, so it never reaches you in the first place.

features.title: Suggested posts gone
features.body: Pages you do not follow, pushed into your feed by the algorithm, stop appearing. Strict mode narrows this to posts explicitly marked "Suggested for you".

features.title: The Sponsored column
features.body: The advertising panel on the right, above your contacts, goes with the rest of it.

features.title: Your people stay put

features.title: See what was caught
features.body: Turn on the placeholder option and each hidden post leaves a small strip with a Show button, so you can check nothing you wanted has been swept up.

features.title: A running count
features.body: The popup keeps a tally of the ads, suggested posts and groups it has hidden for you, with Copy report, Show all and Reset underneath.

faq.q: It hid a post I wanted to see.
faq.a: Facebook shows a Follow button on any page post you do not already follow, including one a friend shared, so those get caught too. Turn on Strict mode and it will only remove posts explicitly marked "Suggested for you". Fewer suggestions disappear, but nothing you actually follow will.
Facebook disguises the labels this relies on and changes the disguise periodically. When that happens ads reappear until the extension is updated. Expected rather than a regression.

faq.q: Does it unfollow or block anything?
faq.a: No. Nothing is blocked, unfollowed or reported on your behalf. Posts are hidden from view and everything returns the moment you switch it off.

faq.q: How do I tell which version is running?
faq.a: Click the extension icon. The version shown is the one actually running in the page. If it does not match what you installed, Chrome is serving an old build. Hit reload on chrome://extensions, then reload Facebook.

extensions.name: Quite for Instagram
extensions.tagline: A feed of the people you actually follow.
extensions.summary: Hides adverts and the suggested posts pushed at you from accounts you do not follow, and does nothing else. What is left is the people you chose.
extensions.metaDescription: Free Chrome extension that hides Instagram adverts and suggested posts from accounts you do not follow. No account, no tracking, nothing sent anywhere.
description: Instagram's feed arrives with two things you did not ask for: posts marked “Ad”, “Sponsored” or “Paid partnership”, and “Suggested for you” posts from accounts you have never followed. Quite for Instagram takes out both and leaves the rest of the app exactly as it was.

A hidden post leaves a small labelled card rather than vanishing outright, which is deliberate rather than a compromise. Instagram reserves scroll space for the posts it has loaded, and closing that gap entirely desynchronises its own height model from what is on screen. Measured on a live feed, collapsing the gap dropped the reader 26,136px past the end of the feed; keeping the card brought that to 223px, and the feed served roughly ten times as much content. A compact card is on by default, shrinking the gap to about a third.
It is built to fail in the safer direction. When Instagram changes its markup, and it does so regularly, the extension lets an advert through rather than hiding a post you wanted to see.
extensions.requires: Chrome, Edge, Brave, Arc, Opera or another Chromium browser.

permissions.name: storage
permissions.why: To remember your checkbox settings, and a running count of what it has hidden. Settings use Chrome's own extension-settings sync, so with Chrome sync on they travel with your Chrome profile. The count stays on the machine it was made on.

hostPermissions.name: *://*.instagram.com/*
hostPermissions.why: The extension runs on Instagram and nowhere else. It has no permission to read any other site, and cannot see any other tab you have open.

features.title: Adverts out of the feed
features.body: Posts marked “Ad”, “Sponsored” or “Paid partnership” are taken out. Detection is an exact string match inside the post's header band rather than a guess at the whole post, so an advert getting through is the failure it is built for, not a post you wanted disappearing.

features.title: Suggested posts, gone
features.body: “Suggested for you” posts come from accounts you have never followed. Untick nothing and they stop arriving. What is left is the people you chose to follow.

features.title: The gap is on purpose
features.body: A hidden post leaves a labelled card the size Instagram reserved for it. Closing that gap sounds better and is worse: it desynchronises the feed's own height model and drops you past the end of what has loaded. A compact card, on by default, shrinks it to about a third.

features.title: Put one back
features.body: Switch on the placeholder and a hidden post leaves a strip with a Show button, so anything taken out can be read anyway. Nothing is ever removed beyond recall.

features.title: One permission, one site
features.body: It asks for storage and nothing else, and runs on instagram.com alone. No account, no server, no analytics, and nothing is sent to us.

options.what: Only hide a post marked “Ad” when it also carries an advertiser's button. Safer, and lets more adverts through.

faq.q: Does it post, like or follow anything?
faq.a: No. It reads the feed to decide what to hide and does nothing else. It cannot act on your account, and it has no permission to reach any site other than instagram.com.

faq.q: Why do hidden posts leave a gap?
faq.a: Because removing it outright breaks the feed. Instagram reserves scroll height for the posts it has loaded, and collapsing that space leaves you scrolling into emptiness while it catches up. The card is the fix, and the compact option makes it small.

Instagram changes its markup regularly, and when it does some posts stop matching until the extension is updated. It is deliberately built to fail that way round rather than hide something you wanted to see.

extensions.name: Quite for Cookies
extensions.tagline: See it before you delete it.
extensions.summary: Shows exactly what a site has stored in your browser, deletes only what you pick, then counts again and tells you what actually went. It can also clear a site on its own when you close its last tab.
extensions.metaDescription: Free, open-source Chrome extension that shows every cookie a site has stored, deletes only what you pick, then checks it actually went.
description: Most cookie cleaners delete first and tell you nothing. Quite for Cookies shows you the list before anything is removed. Every cookie the site has stored, grouped by the domain that set it, with sizes. The ones that keep you signed in are marked as such, and left alone unless you say otherwise. Local storage, databases, caches and service workers are listed alongside them.

Removal is cookie by cookie rather than a blunt sweep of the whole site, so unticking a domain genuinely spares it. Afterwards the extension counts again and reports the result: how many went, how many could not be removed, and how many the page has already set again because it is still open. Those numbers come from re-reading the browser, never from assuming the delete worked.

It can also do the job without being asked. Turn on “clear a site when I close its last tab” and the sweep runs in the background as you browse, sparing sign-ins and anything on your spared list. Chrome’s own session-only setting cannot do this. It waits until you close the whole browser. Every sweep is recorded and shown in the popup, so a run that cleared nothing can never be mistaken for one that worked.
extensions.requires: Chrome, Edge, Brave, Arc, Opera or another Chromium browser.

permissions.name: activeTab
permissions.why: To read the address of the tab you are on when you click the icon, so everything can be scoped to that one site. Nothing is read from the page until you press a button.

permissions.name: cookies
permissions.why: To list and delete cookies. This is what the extension is for.

permissions.name: browsingData
permissions.why: To clear local storage, databases, caches and service workers, restricted to the site you are looking at.

permissions.name: scripting
permissions.why: To run a short read-only snippet in the page that counts the cookies the page itself can see. This is what makes the preview accurate rather than approximate. On a news site you have ticked, the same permission hides the named pop-up boxes and counts them. It reads nothing from the page either way.

permissions.name: storage
permissions.why: To remember which domains you have chosen to spare on each site, and the totals shown in the popup. Nothing leaves your browser.

hostPermissions.name: None at install
hostPermissions.why: Unlike the other two, this one starts with no access to any site at all. When you press “Show what this site stored”, it asks for the one domain you are on, and nothing else. Clearing sites automatically as you close them does need browser-wide access, because it has to see which site a closing tab belonged to. That one is asked for separately, only if you switch it on, and taken back from the same line of text in the popup.

features.title: The list comes first
features.body: Every cookie the site has stored, grouped by the domain that set it, with sizes. Nothing is removed until you have seen it and pressed the button.

features.title: Sign-in cookies are marked
features.body: The ones holding your session are flagged and spared by default, so cleaning a site does not quietly log you out of it.

features.title: Cookie by cookie, not all or nothing
features.body: Untick a domain and it is genuinely left alone. No blunt “clear everything for this site” that takes your other subdomains with it.

features.title: It checks afterwards
features.body: After deleting it counts again and reports what actually went, what could not be removed, and what the page has already set again because it is still open.

features.title: Clear a site as you close it
features.body: Switch it on and closing a site’s last tab clears it, in the background, without you doing anything. Sign-ins and anything on your spared list are left alone, and a second tab still open on the same site stops the sweep.

features.title: Every sweep is recorded
features.body: The background job runs where nobody is watching, so it writes down what it did. A sweep that removed nothing says so, rather than looking the same as one that worked.

features.title: Or sweep the whole browser
features.body: A second tab cleans every site at once. The default removes advertising and analytics cookies only, matched against known tracking domains. It cannot sign you out, because nothing you can log in to is on that list.

features.title: Your cookie-consent answers survive
features.body: Clearing a site used to delete the cookie remembering your answer to its “accept cookies?” box, so the box came back everywhere. Those answers are kept by default now, beside your sign-ins, and you can untick that if you would rather they went. Sites that store the answer somewhere other than a cookie will still ask.

features.title: Pop-ups on news sites, one paper at a time
features.body: Twenty UK papers as tick boxes, plus a box for any other site. Tick one and its “accept cookies?” box and the paper's own subscribe and sale pop-ups are hidden, and the page they were sitting on top of is unlocked. It answers nothing on your behalf, and paid articles stay paid.

features.title: No access until you ask
features.body: It installs with no permission to see any site. Access is requested a site at a time, at the moment you press the button, and is reversible from the popup. The automatic clear is the exception, because clearing sites as you close them has to see which site a closing tab belonged to, so that one asks for every site and is taken back from the same line.

options.what: Advertising and analytics cookies. Cannot sign you out.

options.name: Pop-ups on news sites

faq.a: Not unless you ask it to. Cookies that hold your session are marked and spared by default, the whole-browser sweep defaults to advertising and analytics cookies only, and the automatic clear keeps sign-ins too. The options that do sign you out say so where you turn them on.

faq.q: What does “clear a site when I close its last tab” actually do?
faq.a: When the last tab for a site closes, it clears that site’s cookies in the background. If you still have the site open in another tab, nothing happens. Sites on your spared list are never touched, and sign-in cookies are kept unless you turn that off. Chrome’s own session-only setting cannot do this. It waits until you close the entire browser.

faq.q: Why does it need access to a site?
faq.a: Chrome’s activeTab permission does not cover the cookies API, so reading a site’s cookies genuinely requires host access. Asking for one registrable domain at the moment you press the button is the narrowest form of that. It is granted per site, and revoked from the same line of text in the popup. The automatic clear is the exception: it has to watch tabs closing, so it needs browser-wide access before it will run.

faq.q: How is this different from clearing cookies in Chrome?
faq.a: Chrome clears without showing you what was there, and works on the whole site. This lists everything first, grouped by the domain that set it, lets you spare individual domains, and counts again afterwards to check the removal actually worked.

faq.q: Some cookies came back straight away.
faq.a: If the page is still open it can set them again the moment they go. The report says so explicitly rather than showing a tick. That is the point of counting a second time. Trackers that keep a copy of your ID in local storage do the same thing, which is what the “also clear stored site data” option is for.

extensions.privacy: Quite for Cookies installs with no access to any website, and asks for one site at a time when you press a button, to clear that site or, on a news site you tick, to hide its pop-ups. Switching on the automatic clear is the exception, because clearing sites as you close them needs access to every site, and it asks first. On a ticked site it hides the named pop-up boxes and counts them, and reads nothing from the page. It sends nothing anywhere. No server, no analytics, no account, no tracking. The only things it stores are your per-site choices, the sites you have ticked for pop-up hiding, the counters shown in the popup, and a short local log of what the automatic clear has done, all in your own browser.

_brand: Icons, accents and popup copy match the shipped extensions as of 27 Aug 2026. The mark is a ring with a tail crossing at 45 degrees, in the product accent on a dark ground — same mark for both, differentiated only by colour. Product accents are for artwork only; the site's action colour stays #0071e3. Never use #DF2A24 or #2B83EE — YouTube red and Meta blue read as impersonation.
